summary.text: A 35-year-old female with no past medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with one day of severe abdominal pain that had worsened over eight hours, with nausea, retching, and no flatus or bowel movement for 24 hours. Blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg and pulse 116 bpm with hemodynamic instability; the abdomen was grossly distended and diffusely tender with a firm to hard upper-quadrant mass and absent bowel sounds.

Resuscitation, analgesia and nasogastric decompression were started. Investigations showed raised inflammatory markers, a negative urine pregnancy test, a large gas-filled viscus on abdominal X-ray, and a limited ultrasound that did not visualise the spleen. Because of worsening distension and deteriorating hemodynamic status, emergency surgery was decided after the risks were explained and consent obtained.

Under general anaesthesia, laparotomy found gross peritoneal contamination with about 2300 mL of purulent fluid, a distended stomach with a 180° longitudinal rotation, a dusky wall and a 4 cm lesser curvature perforation, a freely mobile large gut lacking attachments, multiple non-inflamed jejunal diverticula, and absent spleen. After oxygen and warm saline sponges the stomach wall showed viability; the volvulus was reduced, the perforation repaired, and gastropexy and colopexy done, leaving the diverticula in situ.
Postoperatively she went to the surgical intensive care unit on ventilatory support, where septic shock was diagnosed. She died on the first postoperative day despite persistent resuscitation.
